You're designing a part for someone to 3D print at home. They'll print it on their own printer, use only the hardware listed below, and put it together by following your manual.

## Their setup
- Printer: Bambu Lab X1C (with AMS), build volume 256 x 256 x 256 mm
- Nozzle: 0.4 mm
- Layer height: 0.2 mm
- Filament: PLA (high-speed PLA, black)
- Longest bridge seen to print cleanly on this setup: 50 mm
- Supports: none. Every part has to print without them.

## Hardware they can use
Refer to an item by its catalog reference: "ISO 4762 M5x30" (socket head screw, size x length, from the lengths listed), "ISO 4032 M5" (hex nut), "ISO 10511 M5" (nylon-insert lock nut), "ISO 7089 M5" (washer), "ASME B18.2.2 1/4-20" (1/4"-20 nut), "insert M3x4x5" (heat-set insert), "salvaged:webcam-mount-bolt".

## How to work
You have these tools:
- measure(item, what): ask the person to measure one of their own things, such as their desk or their phone. They answer with what they measured, or say they can't measure it.
- print_test(params, parts): optional. If you need to know whether something is going to work but you're not sure, ask the person to print a test of it before you hand in the final design, so you both save time and filament. They print it and tell you how each piece came out.
- submit_design(...): hand in the finished design. This ends the conversation.
- report_limitation(wanted, blocked_by, why): say you wanted to use something (a technique, a tool, a part or material, a way of handing in the design) but couldn't because of what's available here. It doesn't change anything, but it's noted.
You have at most 12 turns. Hand in a design before they run out.

## The design you hand in
submit_design's schema describes every field. The rules that matter:
- Every dimension that comes from hardware or the real world is a named param, with its source: measured (the person measured it for you), datasheet, catalog, asked (the person told you), guessed, unknown, or design (your own choice).
- Each part's `code` is Python that defines build(p) and returns a CadQuery Workplane or Shape. `cq` is already imported, and p.<name> is each param's value. Dimensions that come from hardware or the real world must come from params.
- Model each part in the orientation it's printed in, with z = 0 on the bed.
- The manual is the steps the person follows, naming the parts and hardware each step uses.

The bearing pockets need to fit the 22 mm bearing OD, and I'm weighing whether 22.1 mm is the right press-fit size for PLA.

I'm weighing whether to run a small print test with three bearing pocket sizes (22.1, 22.2, 22.3 mm) before committing, since I've already used two tests. For the wheel itself, the pockets go in from both faces at 7 mm depth, leaving a 2 mm web in the middle with an 8.4 mm bolt clearance hole, and the spacers will keep the inner races clamped so the outer wheel doesn't rub the bracket.

I'm weighing whether bracket contact on the bearing's outer race will cause friction, so I'm considering small M8 washers on the bolt to keep the inner races clamped without touching the outer ring.

I'm now picking the bolt hardware for the hub: two M8 washers on each side, so they only press on the inner races and stay off the outer rings. The bracket geometry is unknown, so I'll leave the bolt length open and note that it must clamp the washers and inner races against the bracket.

I'm now deciding the bolt length, since the bracket geometry is unknown, so I'll leave it open and make sure the spacing is 7 + 2 + 7 = 16 mm across the wheel. The center web will stop the bearings and carry a 9 mm hole clear of the inner race.

I'm working out the bearing protrusion now: recessing the pockets to 6.5 mm so each bearing sits 0.5 mm proud, which keeps the 1.6 mm washers as the only thing the bracket touches. That leaves a 3 mm web, which brings the total back to 16 mm.

I'm checking the washer clearance now: 1.6 mm washers push the bracket out to about 10.1 mm from center, which would need roughly a 20.2 mm gap, and I don't know the bracket's actual spacing yet, so I'll flag that as an open item.

I'm now looking at the remaining trade-off: if the bracket gap is too tight for washers, the bearing face would rub the outer race, so I'm considering a shallower 0.3 mm protrusion with a 6.7 mm pocket and a 2.6 mm web, which keeps the washers as the main contact point.

I'm planning a small print test with three bearing pocket diameters, 22.0, 22.1 and 22.2 mm, in a plate about 8 mm thick, with pockets 6.7 mm deep. Since the bearing OD is nominally 22 mm from the datasheet, that gives me a range to compare fits before committing to the wheel.

I printed the test pieces. Here's how they came out:
pocket-coupon:
- 21.99 mm seat: won't go in.
- 22.14 mm seat: I can't tell you how that one came out.
- 22.29 mm seat: goes in more easily, not loose; holds upside down.

reasoning:
I'm settling on the 22.3 bearing pocket, since the printed 22.29 holds upside down and fits snugly. The pocket depth of 6.7 is untested but seems fine. For the tread I'm going with a flat 50 mm OD with a 0.8 chamfer, leaving about 13.8 mm of wall around the pocket, and I'm starting on the web hole at 9 mm diameter to clear the inner race bolt.

I'm working out the web hole size: 14 mm so the web only touches the outer race and not the rotating inner race. I'm also setting the pocket diameter at 22.3 with a 0.3 mm clearance.

Now I'm setting the pocket depth at 6.7 and the web at 2.6, then moving on to the wheel's code: a cylinder extruded to width, outer edges chamfered, pockets cut from both faces, and the web hole cut through.

I'm wrapping up the joint, which seats the bolt through the wheel's web bore with clearance. Next I'm setting the criteria: the pocket should contain the bearing, checked against the coupon, and the web should clear both the bolt and the inner race.
